transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what finally made me come in is this thing with the historical society. I sort of… took over the fundraiser, or tried to. I was acting like I could run the whole thing myself—making quilt designs, calling all these volunteers, drawing up schedules, promising people deadlines. And then, of course, it was way more than one person could do.

I used to help with sewing projects years ago, my aunt had this old quilting frame in her dining room, and I kept thinking, “Oh, I know how this should go.” But I got carried away. I just kept adding more and more, and now I’ve made a bit of a mess of it.
Has this kind of thing, where you take on too much and then struggle, happened to you before?

Yes, I think so… this fundraiser is just the clearest example because it’s all out in public now. I started with just helping a little, and then suddenly I was doing quilt patterns, calling people, making schedules, telling everyone when things would be done—like I was in charge of the whole thing.

I’ve had that sort of thing happen before, where I get very sure I can handle everything. It reminds me of my aunt’s quilting frame, actually—she could keep a whole room of women organized without even raising her voice. I suppose I thought I could do that too. But then I promise too much, and it turns into more than I can really manage.
Do you find that this pattern of taking on too much and then struggling is something that happens in other areas of your life, not just with the historical society?

Well… yes, I suppose it does, though the historical society one is the one everyone can point to. I started out just helping, and then I was making quilt designs, calling volunteers, writing schedules, promising deadlines—like I could run the whole fundraiser myself.

And quilting is funny, you know, because once you start laying out the pieces, you think, “Oh, I can see the whole pattern,” but then there are all these little seams and corners you didn’t account for. That’s sort of how I get. I see the big plan and jump in, and then suddenly I’ve said yes to far more than I can actually finish.
Do you feel like you need to do things perfectly, or that if you don't, something bad will happen?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I do like things to look right, especially with sewing—my aunt always said if your corners don’t meet, the whole quilt tells on you. But I don’t know that I think something terrible will happen.

It’s more like… I get caught up in how it ought to be, and then I start fussing over the design or the schedule, and before I know it I’m talking about fabric choices when someone only asked me what time the meeting starts. So perfection, maybe, but not in a “bad thing will happen” way. More like I lose the thread a bit.
Do you feel like you need to be in charge of situations to feel comfortable?

I don’t know if it’s being in charge exactly. I don’t sit there thinking, “I have to run this or I won’t be comfortable.” It’s more that if nobody seems to know what’s happening, I start filling in the blanks.

Like with a sewing circle, if the thread and scissors and patterns are all scattered around, someone has to put them in order—or at least that’s what my mind does. My aunt used to have little tins for every color of button, and I always admired that. But then I suppose I can get carried away and start deciding where everyone’s buttons ought to go, even if they didn’t ask me.

So… maybe I feel better when there’s a plan. I’m not sure I’d say I need to be in charge, though.
Do you feel like your tendency to take on too much and then struggle is causing you a lot of stress or problems in your daily life?

Yes… I mean, I suppose it is causing problems. More than I like to admit.

My husband has had to pick up a lot of the house routines lately—things I always used to keep track of, like what needs doing and who’s supposed to be where, that sort of thing. And with the historical society… well, he’s had to deal with some of that too, because I stopped keeping up with what I’d promised. I just couldn’t face people waiting on me, asking where things were.

It’s embarrassing, really. I start out thinking I’m helping, and then it turns into this big tangled spool of thread, and suddenly I don’t want to answer the phone.
Do you often feel anxious or worried about things?

I’m not sure… I mean, I worry about things, but I don’t know if it’s more than anybody else would. There’s always something to think about, isn’t there? Bills, family, whether I remembered to put the good scissors back where they belong—my aunt had a pair she’d practically guard with her life.

But anxious… I don’t know. Sometimes I get wound up when things feel unfinished, or when I think I’ve left someone waiting. Then again, I can spend half an hour fretting over a pattern piece and forget what I was upset about in the first place. So yes, maybe some worry, but I’m not sure how to measure “often.”
Do you often have recurring thoughts or ideas that you feel compelled to act on?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I do get little ideas stuck in my head sometimes, like “I should sort that drawer” or “I need to call so-and-so,” but I don’t know that I feel compelled exactly.

It’s funny, because my aunt used to say if a thought keeps tapping at the window, you might as well let it in—but she was talking about quilting patterns, not anything serious. Sometimes I’ll start with one thought and then it turns into three other things, and before I know it I’m standing in the pantry wondering why I came in there.

So… recurring thoughts, maybe in the ordinary sense. But feeling forced to act on them? I don’t really know. I haven’t noticed anything like that in a clear way.
Do you think your tendency to take on too much and then struggle is more about wanting everything to be perfect or more about wanting to be in control of the situation?

I don’t know… I’m not sure it’s either of those exactly. Perfect, control—those both sound a bit stronger than how it feels in my head.

I think sometimes I just get carried along by the idea of doing something useful, or not disappointing someone. And then, well, once you’ve said yes, it’s like when you start pulling one thread and the whole hem comes loose. My mother used to say you should never agree to alter a dress before you’ve looked at the seams properly, and I suppose that applies to other things too.

So… I don’t know if it’s perfection or control. I haven’t really thought of it that way. It just feels like I mean well, and then I’ve made a mess of too many promises.
Do you think you would still take on so many tasks if you knew someone else was in charge and would handle any mistakes that might happen?

Maybe… I mean, if someone else were really in charge, maybe I’d tell myself I didn’t have to do quite so much. But then I think of the historical society fundraiser, and I just sort of stepped into it like I could run the whole thing myself.

I was starting quilt designs, calling volunteers, making schedules, telling people things would be ready by certain dates… and honestly, those dates weren’t realistic. I think I just got swept up. My aunt used to say a quilt looks simple until you’re the one matching all the corners, and that’s sort of how it was. Before I knew it, I’d promised more than I could possibly get done.
Do you think you would feel less motivated to take on tasks if you didn't feel responsible for their outcome?

I suppose… yes, maybe I would feel less driven if it truly wasn’t on me. But with the historical society fundraiser, I acted like the whole thing was mine to carry.

I started making quilt designs, calling volunteers, putting together schedules, telling people we’d have things done by certain dates—and then, well, those dates were not realistic. It was like I’d decided I could run the whole fundraiser myself, the way my aunt would take over a church supper and suddenly be stirring three pots at once.

So I don’t know if “responsible” is exactly the word, but once I felt like it was mine, I just kept adding more and more.
Do you feel a strong need to have things organized and in their place?

I don’t know that I’d call it a strong need. I like things to be findable, I suppose—scissors in the drawer, thread where it belongs—but then everybody likes that, don’t they?

Though my sewing basket is never as neat as my mother’s was. She had these little tins for buttons, all sorted by color, and I used to think that was just the height of civilization. Mine starts that way and then somehow there are receipts and cough drops in there too.

So… organized and in their place? I’m not sure. I notice when things are a mess, but I don’t know if I need it that way.
Do you think you would be less likely to take on a task if you thought someone else could do it better than you?

Maybe… normally I might step back if someone was clearly better at something. I mean, I know when someone else can bake a pie better than me—my cousin could make a crust that practically sang, and mine always shrinks in the pan.

But with the heritage quilts, no, I didn’t really think that way. I truly believed my ideas were going to put our little town on the map, like I’d finally found the one thing only I could make happen. It sounds a little grand saying it now, but at the time it felt obvious to me.
Do you think you would be less likely to take on tasks if you weren't afraid of them not turning out well?

I’m not sure I’ve thought about it that way. I mean, I do worry how things will turn out sometimes, sure, but whether that’s what makes me take something on or not… I don’t know.

With some things I just get it in my head that it needs doing, and then I’m already halfway into it before I’ve really asked myself why. Like when you start cleaning one cupboard and suddenly all the dishes are on the floor and you find that chipped mug from the county fair—then you’re stuck finishing, aren’t you?

So… if I wasn’t afraid it wouldn’t turn out well, would I take on less? I don’t really know. That’s a hard one to separate out.
Do you think the fear of not doing something well is what drives you to take on and then try to control so many tasks?

I’m not sure it’s fear, exactly. Maybe sometimes, but I don’t notice myself thinking, “Oh, I’d better do this or it’ll be ruined.” It’s more like… I get a picture in my head of how it should go, and then I start fussing with all the pieces.

But “control” sounds so harsh, doesn’t it? My mother used to say my aunt controlled Thanksgiving because she had a certain way the gravy boat had to be placed, and honestly the gravy was the least of everyone’s problems that year because the oven door wouldn’t shut right.

So I don’t know. I may take over more than I realize, but whether that’s because I’m afraid of doing it badly… I can’t really say.
Do you think you would still try to manage every detail of a project if you felt confident that it would succeed without your direct involvement?

I want to say yes, I’d step back if I really trusted it would all go fine… but with that historical society fundraiser, I didn’t. I just sort of jumped in like I could run the whole thing myself.

I was sketching quilt designs, calling volunteers, making schedules, telling people we’d have things done by certain dates—dates that, looking back, I had no business promising. It reminds me of when my neighbor decided we should all do a block party and somehow I ended up knowing who was bringing napkins and who had the folding tables, except this was much bigger.

So… even if someone told me it would succeed without me, I probably still would’ve been in every corner of it, fussing and arranging, because once I got going I felt like it all had to keep moving through me.
Do you feel like your efforts are ever truly good enough, or do you always find something that needs improvement?

I don’t know that I’d say “always.” That sounds so final, like when someone says they’re “always” on time and then you remember the church picnic where they came in after the potato salad was already warm.

I do notice things, though. Little things. A crooked edge, or something that could be clearer, or a phone call I should’ve made sooner. But whether that means I think nothing is ever good enough… I’m not sure. Sometimes I can leave it alone, and other times I keep picking at it.

I guess I haven’t really separated out whether I’m improving something because it truly needs it, or just because I’ve gotten my mind stuck on it.
Do you feel like you're trying to make everything perfect when you take on a task?

Perfect is a funny word. I don’t know if I’m thinking “perfect” exactly. I mean, I do like things done a certain way, but then again, who doesn’t? My sister used to fold towels with the edges all lined up, and I never cared about that, but if it’s a flyer for something, suddenly I care about the margins like they’re holding the whole world together.

So… maybe sometimes I’m trying to get it just right. But I don’t really sit there saying it has to be perfect. I just notice one more thing, and then one more thing after that, and before I know it I’ve spent half the afternoon adjusting something that probably looked fine to everyone else.
Do you think you would be satisfied with a task if it was completed adequately, but not perfectly?

I’m not sure. “Adequately” is one of those words that sounds sensible when you say it in an office, but then when I’m actually looking at the thing, I start wondering who decided what adequate means.

Like if the chairs are set out and the sign is readable and people know where to go, that should be enough, right? But then I’ll notice the sign is a little crooked, or the wording could be warmer, and suddenly I’m thinking about the bake sale at the elementary school years ago where someone wrote “brownies” with an apostrophe and I remember that bothered me more than it should have.

So I guess… sometimes I could be satisfied if it was basically done. Other times I’d probably keep circling back to fix one more thing, even if nobody else cared.
Do you think your actions are more driven by wanting things to be perfect or by wanting to be in control of the situation?

I don’t know if I can separate those two very cleanly. Wanting it perfect and wanting control sort of sit at the same table, don’t they? Like when you’re trying to serve dinner and everyone’s in the kitchen opening drawers and asking where the napkins are, and suddenly you’re not even thinking about dinner anymore, you’re thinking, “Please just let me do this my way.”

But then there are times I’m not trying to control anybody. I’m just fussing with the thing itself. The wording, the order, the little details. So… I’m not sure. Maybe sometimes it’s about control, but I don’t always notice it that way in the moment. It just feels like trying to make things come out right.

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I took on the historical society project like I could run the whole fundraiser myself, starting quilt designs, calling volunteers, making schedules, and promising deadlines I couldn't possibly meet.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about taking over and managing many details of a project, which most directly matches the increased goal-directed activity around running the fundraiser and taking on too much.

patient.answer:
I want to say yes, I’d step back if I really trusted it would all go fine… but with that historical society fundraiser, I didn’t. I just sort of jumped in like I could run the whole thing myself.

I was sketching quilt designs, calling volunteers, making schedules, telling people we’d have things done by certain dates—dates that, looking back, I had no business promising. It reminds me of when my neighbor decided we should all do a block party and somehow I ended up knowing who was bringing napkins and who had the folding tables, except this was much bigger.

So… even if someone told me it would succeed without me, I probably still would’ve been in every corner of it, fussing and arranging, because once I got going I felt like it all had to keep moving through me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a need for perfection
doctor.question: Do you feel like your efforts are ever truly good enough, or do you always find something that needs improvement?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about perfectionism or feeling that work is never good enough, which is not directly covered by the listed Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d say “always.” That sounds so final, like when someone says they’re “always” on time and then you remember the church picnic where they came in after the potato salad was already warm.

I do notice things, though. Little things. A crooked edge, or something that could be clearer, or a phone call I should’ve made sooner. But whether that means I think nothing is ever good enough… I’m not sure. Sometimes I can leave it alone, and other times I keep picking at it.

I guess I haven’t really separated out whether I’m improving something because it truly needs it, or just because I’ve gotten my mind stuck on it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a need for perfection
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're trying to make everything perfect when you take on a task?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about perfectionism when taking on tasks, which is not directly covered by the listed Bipolar I symptom profiles. It does not specifically ask about increased goal-directed activity, mood, sleep, guilt, or other listed symptoms.

patient.answer:
Perfect is a funny word. I don’t know if I’m thinking “perfect” exactly. I mean, I do like things done a certain way, but then again, who doesn’t? My sister used to fold towels with the edges all lined up, and I never cared about that, but if it’s a flyer for something, suddenly I care about the margins like they’re holding the whole world together.

So… maybe sometimes I’m trying to get it just right. But I don’t really sit there saying it has to be perfect. I just notice one more thing, and then one more thing after that, and before I know it I’ve spent half the afternoon adjusting something that probably looked fine to everyone else.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a need for perfection or control
doctor.question: Do you think you would be satisfied with a task if it was completed adequately, but not perfectly?

target_item.reason: The question is about perfectionism or satisfaction with adequate versus perfect task completion, which is not directly covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. “Adequately” is one of those words that sounds sensible when you say it in an office, but then when I’m actually looking at the thing, I start wondering who decided what adequate means.

Like if the chairs are set out and the sign is readable and people know where to go, that should be enough, right? But then I’ll notice the sign is a little crooked, or the wording could be warmer, and suddenly I’m thinking about the bake sale at the elementary school years ago where someone wrote “brownies” with an apostrophe and I remember that bothered me more than it should have.

So I guess… sometimes I could be satisfied if it was basically done. Other times I’d probably keep circling back to fix one more thing, even if nobody else cared.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a need for perfection or control
doctor.question: Do you think your actions are more driven by wanting things to be perfect or by wanting to be in control of the situation?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about perfectionism versus need for control, which is not directly covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I can separate those two very cleanly. Wanting it perfect and wanting control sort of sit at the same table, don’t they? Like when you’re trying to serve dinner and everyone’s in the kitchen opening drawers and asking where the napkins are, and suddenly you’re not even thinking about dinner anymore, you’re thinking, “Please just let me do this my way.”

But then there are times I’m not trying to control anybody. I’m just fussing with the thing itself. The wording, the order, the little details. So… I’m not sure. Maybe sometimes it’s about control, but I don’t always notice it that way in the moment. It just feels like trying to make things come out right.
